I'm mapping out the branch conditions in JsonTreeWriter's get() and put() methods to make sure my JUnit 4 tests cover both true/false paths, including the compound condition around null serialization and pending name checks.

Continuing through the class methods, I'm tracing branches for beginArray/endArray, beginObject/endObject, name(), and the various value() overloads—especially the compound checks in endArray/endObject involving stack emptiness and pending names, the type checks against JsonArray/JsonObject, and the lenient/NaN/infinite validation logic in the double and Number value methods.

Now I'm sketching out the test case plan: verifying get() behavior for empty vs non-empty stacks, checking put() logic for simple values versus pending names, and covering the null-value handling depending on whether serializeNulls is enabled.

Then I'm covering array-nesting and endArray edge cases: calling it on an empty stack throws, calling it with a pending name set throws before checking type, calling it when the top element is an object instead of an array throws, and calling it properly on a matching array succeeds.

Next I'm working through endObject with the same pattern: empty stack throws, a pending name still set throws, top element being an array instead of object throws, and proper matching succeeds. Then I move to name() -- calling it with an empty stack throws, calling it when a pending name is already set throws, calling it when the top isn't an object throws, and calling it correctly on an object sets the pending name without error.

Then I turn to value handling: passing null for a string value inside an object should trigger nullValue() and produce JsonNull (checking behavior based on serializeNulls), while a non-null string at the top level should produce a JsonPrimitive. I also check that nullValue() at the top level yields JsonNull.INSTANCE by default, and that value(true) produces a JsonPrimitive wrapping the boolean, before moving into double value tests.

Now I'm covering the double and Number overloads of value(): with lenient mode enabled, NaN and infinite doubles should pass through without exception, but with the default non-lenient mode they should throw IllegalArgumentException, and normal doubles and longs should just produce the expected JsonPrimitive. The same lenient/non-lenient exception behavior applies when passing a null or NaN/infinite Number object, while a normal Number like an Integer should produce a valid primitive.

Then I'm testing flush() as a no-op that shouldn't throw, and close() behavior: closing with an empty stack should succeed and push a SENTINEL_CLOSED marker, closing with a non-empty stack (like after beginArray()) should throw an IOException, and any operations attempted after closing should fail because the stack is no longer in a valid empty state.

I also want coverage for nested arrays with mixed value types, complex objects, and calling value() after close to confirm it throws similarly to other post-close operations.

Now I'm setting up JUnit4 test structure with the standard imports and confirming the JsonTreeWriter API inherits setLenient/isLenient and setSerializeNulls/getSerializeNulls from JsonWriter, and noting the write methods declare IOException in their signatures even though the actual failures are runtime exceptions.

I'm planning assertions using isJsonPrimitive(), getAsString(), and isJsonNull() checks to verify results, and making sure incomplete object/array test cases properly close out with endObject/endArray so pending state doesn't leak between tests.

I'll set up a @Before method to create a fresh JsonTreeWriter instance for each test, then write out the test methods covering lenient NaN number handling and value(Number) branch behavior depending on the leniency flag.

For the value(double) branch, I need to cover cases like lenient with NaN not throwing, non-lenient with NaN throwing, non-lenient with Infinite throwing, and a normal value passing regardless of leniency.

Now I want to write the test for calling value() directly after beginObject() without setting a pending name, expecting an IllegalStateException since the object top has no pending name.

I'll use JUnit's expected exception attribute for most cases to keep tests concise, then assemble everything into the final test class.

The libraries listed only include JUnit and Hamcrest, but gson core classes are clearly required since the target class imports com.google.gson.*—I'll assume gson is already on the compile classpath as the source under test itself.

Checking the close behavior: after a successful close, the stack holds SENTINEL_CLOSED, so a subsequent get() throws IllegalStateException since the stack isn't empty, and calling close() twice throws IOException on the second call for the same reason.

This is actually a quirky existing behavior worth testing directly—close() twice throws IOException even though it's already closed, which looks like a genuine discovered fault, so I'll include it as a branch coverage test since it's triggered by close() itself leaving a non-empty state.
